variants.headline: Allies join the war against {{opponent}}
body: A column of {{allies}} arrived at our camp before dawn, and their banners now fly beside ours against {{opponent}}. The cooks had to borrow pots from the infantry to feed them all. {{opponent}} will find its next battle more crowded than the last.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: A warning for our other rivals
body: {{allies}} have brought their army into the field against {{opponent}}, and the promise behind that march was made long before this war. A treaty that is never tested is only a pleasant memory; this one has now been tested in public. Every chancellery in the world is revising its estimate of what our signature is worth.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: The pact answered in arms
body: Dispatches from the capital confirm that {{allies}} have entered the war at our side against {{opponent}}. The keeper of the frontier post has added their colors to the board, though he had to move ours to make room. We hope the arrangement proves as durable as the paper it was written on.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Hear it! We do not fight alone
body: Make way! {{allies}} have come to our side and march against {{opponent}}! Their drums were heard on the north road this morning! Our friends have not left us to fight alone! Pass the word to every street!{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Barbarians in sight of {{cityName}}
body: Smoke from the raiders' fires has been rising beyond the ridge above {{cityName}}, and the watch counts {{barbarians}} of them. The last farm outside the wall was abandoned at midday, its door still open. The garrison has shut the north gate and sent for help.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Raiders at the walls
body: Raiders on the ridge! {{barbarians}} of them, and the watch has seen their fires! Drive the herds inside and bar every shutter! Let no child stray past the gate! We hold the wall! We hold the wall!

variants.headline: The herdsmen reach {{cityName}} without the herds
body: The farmer's cart came through the gate at a gallop with an empty harness trailing behind it. Raiders are camped near {{cityName}}, {{barbarians}} by the watch's count, and the ridge glows with their fires each night. 'The oxen bolted before I did,' the farmer said. 'I did not wait to argue.'

variants.headline: Counting raiders at {{cityName}}
body: The watch has fixed a figure on the raiders around {{cityName}}: {{barbarians}}. A band of that size must scatter to feed itself, which means the farms outside the wall will suffer before the town does. Driving them off is a bill the harvest can barely cover, and the town will pay it in grain either way.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, the garrison answers: {{posture}}
body: {{cityName}}'s town book lists raiders in the fields, {{barbarians}} by the watch's count. The captain's answer is written in the margin: {{posture}}. That evening the outer farms were emptied and the gate was barred before the stars appeared.

variants.headline: {{city}} goes hungry under siege
body: Food in {{city}} is running short, and the siege has begun to show at every table. A porter at the grain exchange says the sacks now weigh less than their labels promise. The city is counting meals by the week, and the count is falling.

variants.headline: Who can still buy supper in {{city}}?
body: Hunger will not distribute itself fairly inside {{city}}. The families who buy flour daily will feel the siege first, while a merchant with a full cellar can wait a month. The market stalls are not empty yet; the real shortage is coin, not grain.

variants.headline: In {{city}}, the queue starts before dawn
body: {{terms.civic.people}} of {{city}}, the baker has begun cutting loaves smaller and saying nothing about it. The queue forms before dawn, and every customer watches the scale. Ask him how long the flour will last, and he answers by tapping the empty barrel behind the counter.

variants.headline: To the faithful of {{city}}: hold fast
body: To the faithful in the besieged city: the granaries are nearly bare and the gates must remain shut. Throw open the shrines to anyone without a warm room, and share what bread you can spare. The season will turn, and what is given now will not be forgotten.

variants.headline: The walls of {{cityName}} are failing
body: Rubble from the walls of {{cityName}} now lies in the streets, and the stone holds only {{wallStrength}} of its {{maxWallStrength}} strength. A carter who passed beneath the gate said he could see the sky through the breach. The defenders have not begun repairs, which suggests they have given up on the outer wall.

variants.headline: An accounting of {{cityName}}
body: City examined: {{cityName}}.
Wall standing: {{wallStrength}} of {{maxWallStrength}}.
Verdict: the next storm will finish what the siege began.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight: heavy damage at {{cityName}}
body: Word from abroad tonight: the walls of {{cityName}} have been reduced to {{wallStrength}} of their {{maxWallStrength}} strength. Engineers say the breach is wide enough to march through. The city still flies its flag, but the stone no longer argues for it.

variants.headline: The walls of a rival come down
body: {{cityName}} belongs to {{civilization}}, and its wall has fallen to {{wallStrength}} of the {{maxWallStrength}} it once carried. Stone in that condition turns a battle into a question of nerve, because the defenders must now choose where to stand. If {{civilization}} has a reserve, this is the week to show it.

variants.headline: Our forces attack before {{cityName}}
body: At dawn our regiments moved against {{cityName}}, and the word passed down the line was {{posture}}. From the wall, the soldiers of {{civilization}} watched the companies form in the fields below. By noon the first ladders were on the ground and the outer pickets had been driven in.

variants.headline: From {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, by arithmetic
body: The order before {{cityName}} has changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the change was not made for show. Someone weighed the stores, the roads and the number of defenders, and chose to spend men rather than wait. The defenders must now decide whether to meet the attack or let the wall absorb it.

variants.headline: The offensive at {{cityName}}, entered
body: In this season our host set itself against {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}. The day's command is entered in the book as {{posture}}. Before the sun stood at noon, the camp had been struck and the engines drawn up in line.

variants.headline: The war moves to {{civilization}}'s streets
body: The attack on {{cityName}} started before the bakers had lit their ovens. Soldiers went by at a run, and one stopped long enough to ask a boy for water. He drank it standing, handed back the cup, and was gone before the boy could ask his name.

variants.headline: Back in the fight near {{cityName}}
body: After weeks of falling back, our army before {{cityName}} has turned to face {{civilization}} again, and the order of the day is {{posture}}. Supply wagons that had been sent to the rear are being loaded once more. The road behind the camp is crowded with men going the other way.

variants.headline: The pullback ends at {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has watched our line retreat and now watches it return, under the word {{posture}}. A withdrawal can buy time, shorten a road, or hide a defeat, and headquarters has not said which it was. The answer will be read in what happens when the two armies meet again.

variants.headline: Our forces are back at the line near {{cityName}}
body: Near {{cityName}} tonight, our troops are moving forward again. Command calls the order {{posture}}. The camps that went dark last month are lit once more, and the supply road is busy after sunset.

variants.headline: The second try at {{cityName}}
body: The army is going back to {{cityName}}, and the {{terms.civic.government}} calls that a recovery. The families who buried sons in the first advance may use a shorter word. Before a new levy is raised, the council should publish what the retreat cost and who ordered it.

variants.headline: The line comes back from {{cityName}}
body: The command before {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, has gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. Our column is pulling back, and the wounded went first. No one on the wall fired as the last wagons left the road.

variants.headline: The withdrawal before {{cityName}}
body: The word before {{cityName}} has moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and with it the ground our soldiers held. Three things went unstated: who gave the order, what it cost, and why. A public that pays for a retreat is owed at least the reason for it.

variants.headline: Letters from the front: {{cityName}}
body: We are informed from the front that our forces before {{cityName}} have passed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The dispatch gives no cause and names no officer. We print the change as it reached us and leave the explanation to those who made it.

variants.headline: The boys are off the front at {{cityName}}
body: At the tram stop, a woman read the notice twice, then folded it and put it in her sleeve. Her son's regiment is among those leaving {{cityName}}, and the {{terms.civic.government}} posted the news before any letter arrived. She said she would put the kettle on early, in case he came that night.

variants.headline: Enemy colors near {{cityName}}
body: Columns under the banners of {{enemies}} have been seen a short march from {{cityName}}. Watchmen counted their fires after nightfall, and the miller has hauled his flour behind the wall. The roads remain open, though the carts that use them have grown scarce.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! The enemy is near
body: Look to the north road! Soldiers of {{enemies}} are coming, and their fires already light the ridge! Bring in the flocks and shut the shutters! No one walks the fields after dark! Pass the word! Pass the word!

variants.headline: Three things an army near {{cityName}} can do
body: A force flying the colors of {{enemies}} has come within a day of {{cityName}}. This is more men than a raiding party needs, which leaves three uses: a siege, a march through the fields, or a screen while the real blow falls elsewhere. Our officers should be asking which, not merely counting.

variants.headline: Enemy troops just showed up near {{cityName}}
body: Enemy troops near the city. Banners: {{enemies}}. Close enough that the watch can name them.

variants.headline: {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed in the field
body: The latest fighting cost the enemy {{count|unit|units}}, all carrying the same standard. Our soldiers have stacked the captured colors beside the gate, and the pile reaches a man's shoulder. It will take the enemy a season to replace what was lost in an afternoon.

variants.headline: The enemy's losses, counted
body: Enemy formations destroyed: {{count}}.
Standards taken: one design, repeated.
Balance of the season: entered in our favor.

variants.headline: {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed in the fighting
body: From the front tonight: our troops have destroyed {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}}. Every one of them marched under a single flag. That flag is not ours.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed
body: Gather and hear the count! {{count}} enemy formations are broken on the field! Their banners fill a cart, and their families will learn the number soon enough! Tell it in the square and sing it in every tavern!

variants.headline: A capital falls, far from home
body: News has come that a capital abroad has been taken by force, {{distance}} from the nearest of our cities. The report arrived with a ship's cargo, and the customs clerk read it twice before entering the duty. The war is far away, but the prices it moves are not.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: After {{cityName}} falls, where do the envoys go?
body: {{cityName}}, the seat of {{loser}}, now answers to {{winner}}. A state can lose its capital and keep its authority, or keep the buildings and lose the habit of command. Watch which envoys still call at which door, and the answer will show itself.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital
body: The year's record states that {{winner}} took by arms the capital of {{loser}}, at a distance of {{distance}} from our own cities. The keeper of the rolls entered the fall beside the accounts of plague and drought. Prayer was ordered for the city's people, and no cause was written.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight, a capital has fallen
body: Abroad tonight, word comes that {{winner}} has seized a capital. That is {{distance}} from the closest of our cities. New maps will be needed by morning, and the embassies will be busy before the week ends.

variants.headline: Peace near our borders
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have ended their war. The closer of the two lies {{nearestDistance}} from our frontier, close enough that our carters know its roads. The toll keepers there have stopped asking travelers where they are headed.

variants.headline: Neighbors at peace again
body: Word has reached this office that {{initiator}} and {{target}} have concluded a peace, and that neither side has announced a price. At the border bridge, the keeper has taken down the barrier and swept the planks. May the quiet last longer than the quarrel did.

variants.headline: The quiet between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: The settlement between {{initiator}} and {{target}} contains no term worth printing, which tells us most of what we need. Wars usually end when one treasury empties or both grow tired of paying. Either explanation points the same way: the fighting stopped because it had become too expensive.

variants.headline: When the neighbors' fire burns low
body: Two loud houses have gone dark, and the lane sleeps at last. {{initiator}} and {{target}} have put out their lamps.

variants.headline: War breaks out near our borders
body: War has broken out between {{initiator}} and {{target}}, and the nearer of them stands {{nearestDistance}} from our border. Farmers along that road have begun moving stock away from the frontier. Our own patrols have been doubled, though no one has ordered them to cross.

variants.headline: A war next door
body: The quarrel between {{initiator}} and {{target}} began {{nearestDistance}} from our border, close enough that smoke would be visible from our watchposts. A war that near changes the price of grain, the safety of roads and the mood of every court in the region. Neutrality is a policy, not a shelter.

variants.headline: {{initiator}} at war with {{target}}
body: War between {{initiator}} and {{target}} tonight. The fighting is close to our frontier. Travelers on the border road are choosing the long way around, and the watchposts are keeping their lamps lit.

variants.headline: Their war, our doorstep
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is being fought {{nearestDistance}} from our farms, and our {{terms.civic.government}} has said almost nothing about it. The {{terms.civic.people}} deserve to know whether our roads, our markets and our sons are exposed. Silence near a burning neighbor is not caution; it is an unannounced choice.

variants.headline: A war nearby, set down
body: In this year {{initiator}} and {{target}} took up arms against each other, at a distance of {{nearestDistance}} from our borders. The frontier scribe noted the smoke before he noted the cause. Our own watch was doubled the same week, and the record gives no order for it.

variants.headline: A capital falls near our own border
body: A capital has fallen near our border: {{winner}} has taken the seat of {{loser}}. Refugees have already been seen on the road, carrying what they could tie to a cart. Our frontier posts are counting them as they pass.

variants.headline: What {{winner}}'s capture means here
body: When {{winner}} took the capital of {{loser}}, it gained more than buildings. It gained the offices, the archives and the habit of obedience that gather in a capital. The question now is whether {{loser}} can govern from somewhere else, or whether the state follows the city.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital near our borders
body: The annals record that {{winner}} captured the capital of {{loser}} in this year. The court scribe wrote the entry in a steady hand and left a space beside it for the terms. That space remains empty, and the border has been quiet since.

variants.headline: A capital just fell near us
body: Capital down: {{winner}} has taken {{loser}}'s seat. It is close to us. Watch the roads.

variants.headline: A town changes hands near our border
body: A town near our border has changed hands. The fighting took place {{distance}} from our own fields, and a different banner hung over its gate by evening. Our patrols have been told to hold their line and watch.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{winner}}
body: {{cityName}} has passed from {{loser}} to {{winner}}, at a distance of {{distance}} from our border. A town that close is a market, a road junction and a warning, depending on who holds it. The next thing to watch is not the flag but the garrison left behind.

variants.headline: Notice from abroad: {{cityName}}
body: Notice is given that {{cityName}}, {{distance}} from our frontier, is now held by {{winner}}. Travelers should expect new tolls and new questions at its gate. Merchants with goods in its warehouses should present their papers before the week is out.

variants.headline: A new flag {{distance}} out
body: {{distance}} from our farms, the flag over the town has changed. {{winner}} took it from {{loser}}, and the market opened the next morning as if nothing had happened. The stallholders have seen conquerors before.

variants.headline: {{neighbor}}'s army now outranks ours
body: The army of {{neighbor}} now outnumbers ours, according to the count kept at the war office. The clerks ran the figures twice before sending them up. No one there would say the gap is small.

variants.headline: The tally of arms
body: Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
The balance: theirs, for the first time this season.

variants.headline: Ask why {{neighbor}}'s army passed ours
body: {{neighbor}} has passed us in the count of arms, and the {{terms.civic.government}} has not explained how. The {{terms.civic.people}} pay for every company we raise, and they are entitled to know what our money bought. Either the count is wrong or the policy is.

variants.headline: The balance of arms has turned
body: In this season the army of {{neighbor}} exceeded our own in number. The war office entered the change without comment, as it enters the weather. The frontier companies were ordered to stand their ground and report.

variants.headline: Our army passes {{neighbor}}'s
body: The war office count now puts our army above {{neighbor}}'s. The new figure was posted on the board, and an officer stood looking at it longer than the others. He said only that the lead would have to be used before it was spent.

variants.headline: Our arms in good order
body: Letters from the war office state that our forces now exceed those of {{neighbor}} in the field. The return was read at the war office and entered without ceremony. A lead in numbers is a tool; what matters is the hand that holds it.

variants.headline: Our army just passed {{neighbor}}'s
body: Count changed: our army is bigger than {{neighbor}}'s now. The board at the war office says so. Somebody should tell the enemy.

variants.headline: The account of strength
body: Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
The balance: ours, by the difference.

variants.headline: {{city}} takes heavy damage
body: The walls of {{city}} have been badly hit and now hold {{wallStrength}} of their {{maxWallStrength}} strength. Dust from the breach has settled on the roofs as far as the market square. The garrison has moved its stores underground and posted extra men at the gap.

variants.headline: The cost to {{city}}
body: {{city}} can still call on {{wallStrength}} of the {{maxWallStrength}} its walls were built to bear, and that is not enough for comfort. A breach changes the arithmetic of a siege: the defender must now watch two lines, the wall and the hole in it. Every hour spent repairing is an hour the attacker also gets to use.

variants.headline: The crack in {{city}}'s wall
body: A mason walked the length of the wall at {{city}} this morning, tapping the stone with a mallet and saying nothing. The section he stopped at holds {{wallStrength}} of its {{maxWallStrength}} strength, and he has asked for lime and a second cart. His apprentice says the old man has not slept since the first strike.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{city}}! The walls are hurt
body: Stand clear of the wall! The stone is cracked and holds only {{wallStrength}} of its {{maxWallStrength}} strength! Keep the children off the rubble and let the masons work! We will mend it, but not if you stand in the way!

variants.headline: Our forces counterattack at {{cityName}}
body: Our forces at {{cityName}} have gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The change came at dawn, with the horns sounding before the mist lifted. By the time the defenders understood it, our leading companies were already across the ground between the lines.

variants.headline: From defense to the strike at {{cityName}}
body: The word at {{cityName}} has shifted from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the army is spending what it saved while waiting. A counterattack works when the enemy has outrun his supplies or his nerve. If neither is true, it is only a louder way to lose men.

variants.headline: Our forces attack at {{cityName}}
body: At {{cityName}} tonight, our forces have moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The horns sounded at first light, and the forward companies went in before the enemy had finished his breakfast. Command says the line is holding.

variants.headline: The defense holds and answers
body: Dispatches from before {{cityName}} report that our forces have passed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The dispatch says the movement began at dawn and was carried out in good order. We print the account as it reached us, with the hope that good order may soon be matched by good news.

variants.headline: The front at {{cityName}} goes defensive
body: The order at {{cityName}} has changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. Soldiers who expected to advance are instead digging, and the wagons have been sent to the rear. The wall is being strengthened at the points where the last attack came closest.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, a stance change unexplained
body: A note from the front at {{cityName}} records a change of posture from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The dispatch offers no reason for the change and no estimate of how long it will last. Our readers may draw their own conclusions from the silence.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Our soldiers stand at the walls
body: To the walls! Our soldiers stand on the walls, and every hand is needed! Bring water, bandages and hot food to the gate! Keep the streets clear and the lamps burning! We hold what we have!

variants.headline: The record of {{cityName}}'s front
body: In this season the command at {{cityName}} passed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The camp was moved closer to the wall, and the men began work on ditches and palisades. The record notes the change and does not explain it.

variants.headline: A war ends in capitulation
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have ended their war, and the settlement is entered as a capitulation. A rider brought the news to the foreign office before the market opened, and the clerks read it in silence. The terms have not been published, so no one can yet say which side bowed.

variants.headline: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is ended
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is over. It began with promises and ended with a signed page, and the record calls the ending a capitulation. What is left is a border to redraw and a generation of letters to answer.

variants.headline: Our war with {{initiator}} ends in capitulation
body: Our war with {{initiator}} has ended, and the record describes the settlement as a capitulation. Whether the terms favor us will be known when they are printed, and the government has not printed them. Until then, the only fact worth holding is that the shooting has stopped.

variants.headline: Our war with {{target}} is settled
body: Peace with {{target}} is signed, and the instrument records a capitulation. At the frontier station, the barrier was raised before noon and the first cart in months crossed without a challenge. We do not yet know the price, but we know the sound of the guns has stopped.

variants.headline: A peace with visible terms
body: The peace terms include {{count}} concessions: {{concessions}}. A broker at the exchange copied the list into his book before he would name a price for anything. The market has taken the paper at its word, which is more than the parties have done.

variants.headline: The terms between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: Signed by: {{initiator}} and {{target}}.
Concessions recorded: {{count}}.
The list: {{concessions}}.

variants.headline: Who owes what in the peace with {{target}}?
body: The peace with {{target}} lists {{concessions}} among its concessions. Each concession is either a payment or a promise, and every household that helps pay can tell the two apart. Let the {{terms.civic.government}} print the full terms, what we gave and what we got, before it asks for another levy.

variants.headline: A peace with terms tonight
body: Peace has been concluded between {{initiator}} and {{target}}. The settlement lists {{count}} concessions. A clerk read the pages aloud at the exchange, and the crowd heard every one.

variants.headline: Peace on one front only
body: The guns facing {{settled}} are silent, and peace has been signed. The war with {{remaining}} goes on, and the regiments from the quiet side are already marching. They have traded one road for another.

variants.headline: One account closes, others stay open
body: {{settled}} has made peace with us, while the war with {{remaining}} goes on. A treaty on one border always frees soldiers for another. Where those soldiers march will tell the country more than any speech from the {{terms.civic.government}}.

variants.headline: Peace with {{settled}}
body: The peace with {{settled}} is concluded, and the bells rang at noon. They stopped sooner than expected, perhaps because the war with {{remaining}} is still burning. We join in the relief and reserve our hopes for the front that has no treaty yet.

variants.headline: Bells for one front, drums for the others
body: The bells have rung for {{settled}}, and the war with {{remaining}} goes on. The families waiting on that front heard the same bells and understood what they meant. Let the {{terms.civic.government}} tell them why one quarrel could be closed and theirs left open.

variants.headline: We are at peace
body: Peace has come to the nation. In the capital, the recruiting table was carried away before noon, and the square filled with people who had no orders to follow. The first carts of returning soldiers are expected within the week.

variants.headline: The record of rest
body: The record notes that the war has ended. The muster rolls were closed, the frontier companies were released to their homes, and the bells were rung in every town that had one. The scribe adds no praise and no blame, only the date.

variants.headline: The long walk home
body: A woman on the east road walked past the recruiting table this morning and stopped, because there was no table. Her husband's regiment is said to be coming home, and she has been carrying a letter in her pocket for a month. She read it again, then went to buy flour for a larger loaf.

variants.headline: Peace, and what to do with it
body: The war is over, and the country has not yet decided what to do with the peace. The men will come home to workshops that closed and fields that went unploughed, and the bills will arrive before the welcome does. A government that can raise an army should be able to plan a harvest.

variants.headline: Please print the names by village
body: Madam, they say the war is over. When the names of those coming home are ready, please set them down by village, so each street can look for its own. My aunt cannot read a whole page, but she knows the shape of one name, and she has been looking for it for two years.

variants.headline: {{count}} of our companies lost in action
body: The latest fighting cost us {{count|company|companies}}. The news reached the war office in a single dispatch, and the clerk who copied it left the room without speaking. The lists of names will take longer to prepare than the count did.

variants.headline: Our losses, counted
body: Companies lost: {{count}}.
Names entered: still being copied.
The account: not yet closed.

variants.headline: The empty bunks
body: At the barracks, the sergeant walked down the row of bunks and did not stop at {{count|company|companies}} of them. The blankets are folded and the kits are gone, and he has not yet asked for replacements. He says the room is quieter than it used to be.

variants.headline: The count from the fighting
body: They say the fighting took {{count}} of our companies. I heard it from a man who was there, and he would not say more than the number. The families will hear the rest soon enough.

variants.headline: Vassals drawn into the war
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has drawn in {{vassals}}, who march under their oaths. Their columns took the road this week, and the inns along it filled by nightfall. A quarrel between two powers has become the work of several.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: What the vassals add
body: {{vassals}} have joined the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} because their oaths require it. A vassal does not choose the quarrel, only the road, so the new names bring soldiers without bringing a cause. No new quarrel has begun; the old one has simply gained more hands.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: The record of vassalage honored
body: The book of oaths sets down that {{vassals}} joined the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} under the bond of vassalage. Their banners went where their master's went, as they have in earlier reigns. The scribe records that the oath was kept and enters no price beside it.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Small kings, big wars
body: {{vassals}} are being marched into a war that {{initiator}} and {{target}} began, and no one asked their opinion. An oath is a grand thing for a great power to hold and a heavy thing for a small one to carry. {{terms.civic.people}}, note who writes these agreements and who is merely written into them.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Our advantage over {{opponent}} stops growing
body: The war against {{opponent}} has stopped gaining ground. The supply clerk still loads the same flour each morning, but now he asks the same provisioners for it twice. The officers at the front cannot say when the line last moved.

variants.headline: The stalled advance against {{opponent}}
body: Reports have been good, yet the count against {{opponent}} has hardly moved. A number that refuses to change may mean a pause, a siege, or an army that has outrun its wagons. The record does not yet choose between them.

variants.byline: A farmer with a son in the ranks
variants.headline: The war that stands still
body: Madam, the war with {{opponent}} has settled around a single camp, and my son's regiment is in that camp. The harvest is brought in by other hands, and the tax collector still finds the doorstep, while the fighting finds nothing to do. Will a counselor tell us what the army waits for, and how long our patience is expected to last?

variants.headline: Stuck: the war with {{opponent}}
body: The line has not moved again this week. The same camps keep sending the same bills.

variants.headline: Two friends go to war
body: {{first}} and {{second}} have gone to war, though both count themselves friends of ours. Their envoys still nod to each other in our capital, but they no longer ride in the same carriage. Our friendship with each never promised them friendship with each other.

variants.headline: When friends fight
body: {{first}} and {{second}} were both our friends, and now they are each other's enemies. Each court will ask what our friendship is worth, and each will judge the answer by what we send the other. An even hand will look like betrayal in both capitals.

variants.headline: A plea in the war of {{first}} and {{second}}
body: It is painful to report that {{first}} and {{second}}, both friends of this nation, have taken up arms against each other. We will not set ourselves up to judge a quarrel whose beginnings are hidden from us. We ask only that our friendship be put to use as a peacemaker before the table is broken past mending.

variants.headline: They say the table is broken
body: The innkeeper keeps the corner table for two envoys who used to share it. Now {{first}} and {{second}} are at war, and each sends his man to a different room. The second cup is still on the shelf, and the girl who dusts it has stopped asking why.

variants.headline: The war runs long
body: This war has now lasted {{turns}}. At the joinery, the master has stopped promising delivery dates, because the men who used to finish the work are still away. He planes the boards himself now, and the shavings pile up by the door.

variants.headline: The long stretch of the war with {{opponent}}
body: The war with {{opponent}} has lasted {{turns}}, and a war of that age is no longer the one its makers declared. The men change, the money changes, and the purpose shifts quietly with them. Whatever is signed at the end will answer a question nobody asked at the start.

variants.headline: The record of a long war
body: The town book sets down the war's length at {{turns}}. In the muster yard, the sergeant now writes down recruits who were not born when the fighting began. The record offers no judgment, only the count.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} is {{turns}} old
body: The bakery has taken down the board where it marked the count. The war with {{opponent}} is {{turns}} old, and nobody at the counter remembers how it started. Everyone knows someone still out there.

variants.headline: The nation is at war
body: The country is at war. Before the clerks had opened their ledgers, a line had formed at the recruiting office, and the first names were written in a borrowed hand. On the frontier, the watch fires burned until dawn.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: {{initiator}} has attacked
body: War, tonight. {{initiator}} has opened war on us. The reserves have been called in, and the frontier garrisons are standing to. We will bring you more as the dispatches arrive.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Hear it! {{initiator}} makes war on us
body: Hear it! {{initiator}} has brought war to our gates! Every man to his post, every gate barred, every storehouse counted! They chose this quarrel, and we will finish it!{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: A state of war with {{target}}
body: This nation and {{target}} are now in a state of war. The {{terms.civic.government}} is said to have weighed the question at length before deciding. The first levy left the yard before this edition was set, and the couriers were still dusty when they passed the window. We hope the weighing was as careful as we are told.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.when: role === 'joined' && reason === 'pact' && initiator !== null && target !== null
variants.headline: Their quarrel, our treaty
body: A treaty has turned the quarrel between {{initiator}} and {{target}} into our own. A pact is a debt taken on in fair weather, and the collector is at the door. {{terms.civic.people}}, ask the council what this war is meant to buy, and ask before the ledgers are closed.{{hostileAllies}}

values.attackers: (() => { const declarations = new Map(merge.members.map(({ incident }) => [incident.initiator.id, incident.initiator])); const named = [...declarations.values()].filter(p => p.knows('name')).map(p => p.name); const unknown = declarations.size - named.length; if (unknown) named.push(unknown === 1 ? 'one unnamed power' : unknown + ' unnamed powers'); return named.join(', '); })()
values.otherFronts: (() => { const declarations = merge.members.map(m => m.incident); const fresh = new Set(declarations.map(i => i.initiator.id)); const first = declarations.reduce((a, b) => b.turn < a.turn ? b : a); const earlier = new Set(first.earlierWarOpponents.map(entry => entry.player.id)); const ongoing = [], other = []; for (const rival of self.wars) { if (!rival.knows('major') || !rival.major || !rival.knows('id') || fresh.has(rival.id)) continue; (earlier.has(rival.id) ? ongoing : other).push(rival.knows('name') ? rival.name : 'an unnamed power'); } return [ongoing.length ? 'Already at war with: ' + ongoing.join(', ') + '.' : '', other.length ? 'Other active fronts: ' + other.join(', ') + '.' : ''].filter(Boolean).join(' ') || 'These declarations account for all active major fronts.'; })()
values.allies: (() => { const named = new Map(); for (const { incident } of merge.members) for (const entry of incident.hostileCityStateAllies) if (entry.player.knows('name')) named.set(entry.player.id, entry.player.name); return named.size ? ' Hostile city-state allies: ' + [...named.values()].join(', ') + '.' : ''; })()

variants.headline: War on {{count|front|fronts}}
body: New declarations reached the capital today from {{merge.values.attackers}}.{{merge.values.allies}}
{{merge.values.otherFronts}} The map room has no wall left for another pin.

variants.headline: War on {{count|front|fronts}}
body: Our enemies now number {{enemies}}. In the map room, the clerk has begun pinning new fronts to the wall because the table is full. Each declaration adds a line to his book and a name to the list of families waiting.

variants.headline: Count the fronts
body: We now fight {{count|war|wars}}, against {{enemies}}, and all of them ask for the same soldiers. Every company sent to one front is a company the others must do without, and the {{terms.civic.government}} has not said which front comes first. Until it does, the army is being divided evenly among quarrels that are not equal.

variants.headline: Hear it! The nation fights on {{count|front|fronts}}
body: Hear the names of those who fight us: {{enemies}}! One country cannot feed so many fronts, so every pair of hands must do the work of two! Bring in the harvest, man the gates, and let them hear that we are still standing!

variants.headline: We are at war with {{count|power|powers}} now
body: War count: {{count|power|powers}}. Names: {{enemies}}. Every front sends its bill to the same purse. You can guess whose.

variants.headline: The war tally favors {{opponent}}
body: The tally in the war with {{opponent}} has fallen to {{score}}. The printer still posts each new figure in his window, but the crowd that used to gather around it has thinned. The ones who stop now ask only whether anyone has opened talks.

variants.headline: The number nobody in the {{terms.civic.government}} quotes
body: The count in the war with {{opponent}} stands at {{score}}, a figure no minister has repeated aloud. Such numbers are not weather. They are the total of orders given and chances refused, and the public that paid for them should hear the arithmetic.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} tonight
body: The war with {{opponent}}, tonight: the count is {{score}}. Officers talk of holding. Nobody talks of advancing.

variants.headline: The record of a hard season
body: The campaign book enters the count against {{opponent}} at {{score}}. The hospital has more wounded than beds, and the cloister has been given over to cots. The book records such seasons without complaint, as it recorded them for our fathers.

variants.headline: Our side leads in the war with {{opponent}}
body: The count in the war with {{opponent}} has risen to {{score}} in our favor. At the post office, the same families still come each week for letters and ask the same question at the window. A good tally has never yet brought a soldier home.

variants.headline: What the lead is worth
body: Our side now leads by {{score}} in the ledger of the war with {{opponent}}. Ground and lives bought that margin, and it is worth only what the other side will pay to stop losing. The price should be tested while the lead is still new.

variants.headline: The war proceeds favorably
body: Merchants are informed that the war with {{opponent}} goes well and that our side holds {{score}} at the exchange. Shipping agents have cut their rates on the eastern run. Traders may plan on that basis.

variants.headline: Good news, and the bill beside it
body: The barkeep has chalked our {{score}} lead over {{opponent}} beside the ale price, and the regulars have begun arguing about the parade route. One man ordered nothing and said he was saving for the celebration. The keeper poured him a glass anyway and put it on the slate.

variants.headline: The war sits lighter on the country
body: The country's weariness has fallen to {{weariness}} in a hundred. On the high street, people talk about roof tiles and the state of the road instead of the front. The shops have more customers than they did a month ago.

variants.headline: Weariness eases in the war with {{opponent}}
body: The country's mood has improved: weariness with the war against {{opponent}} stands at {{weariness}} in a hundred. At the coach office, travelers have begun asking after the southern road again, and the morning coach has gone out full all week. A people that can look past a war may yet be able to end it.

variants.headline: The number behind the mood
body: The nation's patience with the war against {{opponent}} has climbed back to {{weariness}}, after a season above the halfway mark. Patience is a store like grain or coin, and this one has just been replenished. What empties or fills that store, more than any battle, sets the length of a war.

variants.headline: Down to {{weariness}}: the country exhales
body: Still at war. The barber says the morning passed without one word about the front. His first complaint was a haircut.

variants.headline: The war begins to wear us down
body: The war against {{opponent}} now weighs on the country at {{weariness}} in a hundred. The cobbler on the east street no longer asks after customers' families; he reads their news in the state of their boots. These days the war is paid for one small repair at a time.

variants.headline: A weary nation, and no statement
body: At {{weariness}} in a hundred, the country's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} has passed the halfway mark. The {{terms.civic.government}} has offered no answer to that mood. In such a season silence is taken as a reply, and not a comforting one.

variants.headline: Tired of the war? Say it plainly
body: {{weariness}} in a hundred: that is how much patience remains for the war against {{opponent}}. Such a figure is a vote cast in kitchens and workshops, long before any council records it. Read it now, before it is expressed in a way no one can ignore.

variants.headline: The record of a weary nation
body: The almshouse book enters the nation's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} at {{weariness}} in a hundred. The line forms before daylight now, and the butcher's hand is heavier on the scale. Patience is not the same as endurance.

variants.headline: Breaking: {{merge.values.distinctAttackers|power|powers}} declare war
body: On day {{key}} the declarations came in a wave. {{merge.values.attackers}} all declared war on us.{{merge.values.allies}}
